slides: Now rows with a rule. Some people must stand together, some must stand apart. Some items repeat. And sometimes the row is a round table.

slides.say: Each rule changes how we count, and each one has its own trick. We'll see each trick on a tiny case first.
Let's start with a tiny case. A, B and C stand in a row. A and B must stand together. How many orders?
at: A, B and C stand in a row

slides.say: Here are all six orders of A, B and C.
A and B are next to each other in A B C, B A C, C A B and C B A. That's four orders.
Now the trick. We glue A and B into one block. Then we have two items, the block and C.
Two items in a row, two factorial, two orders.
And inside the block, A and B can stand in two orders, A B or B A.
Two times two is four. The same four orders.
Now a new example. Five friends stand in a row. Dan and Mia must stand together.
at: Five friends stand in a row

slides.say: We glue Dan and Mia into a block. The block and the three other friends are four items. Four factorial is twenty-four.
Inside the block, Dan and Mia can stand in two orders.
Twenty-four times two is forty-eight. Don't forget the order inside the block.
Now the opposite rule, apart. Back to A, B and C. Now A and B may not stand together.
Apart is everything except together. All six orders, minus the four together. Six minus four is two.
Now a new example. Four friends in a row, and Dan and Mia must stand apart.
All the orders, four factorial, twenty-four.
Together, we glue them. Three items, three factorial, six. Times two inside the block, twelve.
All minus together. Twenty-four minus twelve is twelve.
There's a second way for apart, the gaps. We place the other two friends first, Ann and Ben. They can stand in two orders.
at: We place the other two friends first

slides.say: Ann and Ben make three gaps. One before them, one between them, and one after them.
Dan goes into one of the three gaps. Mia goes into one of the two other gaps. That way they're never next to each other.
at: Dan goes into one of the three gaps

slides.say: Two times three times two is twelve. The same twelve. [pause] Okay. I'll see you in the next part.
